passages.text: Previous studies showed that induction of necroptosis by pan-caspase inhibitors in BMDMs requires priming with LPS or TNF. However, on the basis of our results, AMs are highly susceptible to necroptosis without any priming. To assess cell type-specific sensitivity to the induction of necroptosis, we compared cultured AMs and M-CSF-derived BMDMs or mouse lung fibroblasts after treatment with emricasan. The results clearly showed robust production of IL-1alpha and cell death in cultured AMs, but not in BMDMs (Fig. 3A, B) or mouse lung fibroblasts (Fig. 3C, D) following treatment.

We then focused on the signal events upstream of RIPK1/RIPK3 activation in the necroptotic cell death. It has been reported that induction of RIPK1-dependent necroptosis typically requires death-domain-related signaling, such as the signal events downstream of TNF-TNFR1 engagement. To clarify the contribution of TNF signaling in these responses, we used cultured AMs from Tnf-/- mice and compared IL-1alpha release and cell death with those of littermate mice. The results revealed no statistically significant difference in the release of IL-1alpha or cell death between cultured AMs from Tnf -/- and those from Tnf +/- or Tnf +/+ mice, suggesting a minimal contribution of TNF-TNFR1 signaling. Alternatively, other death-domain receptor-related ligands may contribute to emricasan-induced necroptosis in cultured AMs (Fig. S8).

Caspase-8 serves as a critical regulator of RIPK1 activity under homeostatic conditions by cleaving RIPK1 to prevent the execution of necroptosis. Furthermore, a previous study reported that caspase-8 is required for M-CSF-dependent differentiation of macrophage precursor without inducing apoptosis. In line with these observations, we detected the mature form of caspase-8 (cleaved caspase-8) in cultured AM and BMDMs lysates in the steady-state condition by western blot analysis (Fig. 3E). The result also clearly showed that the level of cleaved caspase-8 decreased in lysates of cultured AMs and BMDMs treated with emricasan (Fig. 3E). Parallel to that, remarkable caspase-8 activity was detected in both AMs and BMDMs, which was impaired by the treatment of emricasan (Fig. 3F). These results show no significant difference in caspase-8 expression and enzymatic function between AMs and BMDMs before and after the treatment of emricasan.

We then compared the gene expression levels of RIPK1 and RIPK3, which are the key molecules in necroptosis downstream of caspase-8 inhibition, in these macrophages by qPCR and found that neither type of macrophage upregulated these genes, and the levels were comparable following treatment with emricasan (Fig. 3G). However, western blot analysis revealed that the accumulation of polyubiquitinated- or phosphorylated-like high molecular weight ladders of RIPK1 and RIPK3, which were remarkable in cultured AMs, was not evident in BMDMs (Fig. 3H).

We then tried to clarify whether the mechanism of emricasan-induced necrosis-like cell death was dependent on caspase-8 inhibition using the caspase-8-specific inhibitor benzyloxycarbonyl (Cbz)-Ile-Glu (OMe)-Thr-Asp (OMe)-FMK (Z-IETD-FMK). Notably, Z-IETD-FMK alone could not induce necroptosis-like cell death (Fig. 3I, J). Therefore, we hypothesized that emricasan would exhibit greater inhibitory efficacy against caspase-8 enzymatic activity than Z-IETD-FMK, and we evaluated this by performing a luminescence-based caspase-8 activity assay. The results demonstrated that the inhibitory potency of emricasan against caspase-8 was not significantly different from that of Z-IETD-FMK (Fig. S9A). We also used a caspase-1 selective inhibitor, VX-765 (belnacasan), a caspase-3/7 selective inhibitor, N-Ac-Asp-Glu-Val-Asp-CHO (Ac-DEVD-CHO), and a mixture of these and found that simultaneous inhibition with these caspases significantly upregulated IL-1alpha release and cell death (Fig. 3I, J). Furthermore, we found that caspase-1 inhibition by VX-765 induced necroptosis-independent cell death, which was not blocked by necrostatin-1 or GSK872 treatment. However, the mixture of caspase-1 -3/7 and -8 inhibitors shifted the death to necroptosis, suggesting that the necroptosis-like cell death required a multiple caspases inhibition rather than a single inhibition of caspases (Fig. S9B).

Collectively, these results demonstrate that AMs are susceptible to RIPK1/RIPK3-mediated necroptosis, and that multiple caspase inhibition is required for the induction of cell death and IL-1alpha release.
Emricasan functions as a pulmonary mucosal adjuvant that induces necroptosis upon airway administration
Emricasan is a mucosal adjuvant that induces necroptosis when administered intranasally.

A-D C57BL/6 WT, Ripk1DN/DN and Ripk3-/- mice received intranasal emricasan (0.8 kg/mL) in PBS. After 10 h, BALF was collected by instilling PBS 500 muL. IL-1alpha levels in BALF were measured using ELISA (A, B) (n = 4-5/group). Neutrophil infiltration into BALF was quantified using a cell analyzer 12 h after emricasan administration (C, D) (n = 3-4/group). The gating strategy for evaluating immune cells in the BALF post-administration is shown in Figs. S11, S12. E, F C57BL/6 WT mice received OVA (10 mug) with or without aluminum hydroxide (alum, 3.3 mg/kg) or emricasan (Emri, 0.8 mg/kg) intranasally on days 0 and 10. On day 17, the mice were sacrificed and serum and BALF were collected. OVA-specific IgG1 (E) (n = 4-5/group) and IgA (F) (n = 9-13/group) titers were analyzed using ELISA. (G-J) C57BL/6 WT and Ripk1DN/DN or Ripk3-/- mice received OVA (10 mug) with or without emricasan (Emri, 0.8 mg/kg) intranasally on days 0 and 10. On day 17, the mice were sacrificed and serum and BALF were collected (G, H: n = 4-8/group, I, J: n = 9-10/group). OVA-specific IgG1 (G, I) and IgA (H, J) titers were analyzed using ELISA. Data were representative of two independent experiments (A-E) or are pooled from two independent experiments (F-J). Error bars represent mean +- SD. P values were calculated with the Kruskal-Wallis test or one-way ANOVA (Tukey's multiple comparisons test). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001, ns (not significant).

To clarify the contribution of necroptosis to IL-1alpha production in a mouse model of respiratory inflammation, we analyzed immune responses in the lungs of WT, Ripk1DN/DN, or Ripk3-/- mice following airway administration of emricasan. As we expected, 6 hours after emricasan administration, IL-1alpha production in the lungs was significantly reduced in the genetically modified mice (Fig. 4A, B). In parallel with IL-1alpha levels, infiltration of neutrophils into the lungs was also significantly reduced in genetically modified mice 12 h after emricasan administration (Fig. 4C, D). These results suggest that emricasan induces necroptosis of AMs in the lungs in the same manner as observed in the in vitro study, and that the released IL-1alpha may function as a pulmonary adjuvant. To assess the potential of emricasan as a pulmonary adjuvant, OVA was administered to the airway of mice via the intranasal route, either alone, in combination with emricasan, or with alum on days 0 and 10. Seven days after the final administration (day 17 of the course), serum and BALF were collected. As shown in Fig. 4E, the group of mice treated with intranasal emricasan showed significant induction of OVA-specific serum IgG1, comparable to that induced by alum. Emricasan also significantly elevated OVA-specific IgA levels in BALF (Fig. 4F). To investigate the contribution of necroptosis to antibody responses, we evaluated the adjuvant effect of emricasan using Ripk1DN/DN and Ripk3-/- mice. The results showed that OVA-specific serum IgG1 and BALF IgA were significantly reduced in Ripk1DN/DN (Fig. 4G, H) and Ripk3-/- mice (Fig. 4I, J), demonstrating that the adjuvanticity of emricasan is almost entirely dependent on RIPK1-RIPK3-mediated necroptosis.
The adjuvanticity of emricasan is mainly dependent on necroptosis-mediated IL-1 release
The adjuvanticity of emricasan is mainly dependent on necroptosis-mediated IL-1 release but has the unique property of reducing IgE production.

A, B C57BL/6 Il1r1+/- and Il1r1-/- mice received OVA (10 mug) with or without emricasan (Emri, 0.8 mg/kg) intranasally on days 0 and 10. On day 17, the mice were sacrificed and serum and BALF were collected (n = 8-11/group). OVA-specific IgG1 (A) and IgA (B) titers were analyzed using ELISA. C-E C57BL/6 WT mice received OVA (10 mug) with or without rIL-1alpha (50 ng) or emricasan (Emri, 0.8 mg/kg) intranasally on days 0 and 10. On day 17, the mice were sacrificed and serum and BALF were collected (n = 9-10/group). OVA-specific IgG1 (C), IgA (D), and IgE (E) titers were analyzed using ELISA. F-J C57BL/6 WT mice received OVA alone, OVA (10 mug) with IL-1alpha (50 ng), or OVA (10 mug) with IL-1alpha (50 ng) with rTNF (100 ng) intranasally on days 0 and 10. On day 17, the mice were sacrificed and serum and BALF were collected (n = 5/group). Serum levels of OVA-specific IgG1 (F), IgE (G), and BALF levels of OVA-specific IgA (H) titers were analyzed using ELISA. The ratios of OVA-specific IgG1/IgE (I) and IgA/IgE (J) were calculated after the levels of each isotype were determined. Data were pooled from two independent experiments (A-E) or are representative of two independent experiments (F-J). Error bars represent mean +- SD. P values were calculated with the Kruskal-Wallis test or one-way ANOVA (Tukey's multiple comparisons test). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001, ns (not significant).

Next, we investigated whether IL-1 release through necroptosis contributes to antibody responses, using IL-1R1-deficient mice. The results showed that both OVA-specific serum IgG1 and BALF IgA were significantly reduced in these mice, indicating that the adjuvanticity of emricasan is largely dependent on necroptosis-mediated IL-1 release (Fig. 5A, B). These results suggest that IL-1alpha, a DAMP released during necroptotic cell death, contributes to the adjuvanticity of emricasan as an effective pulmonary mucosal adjuvant. To confirm the potential of IL-1alpha as a pulmonary mucosal adjuvant, we performed a side-by-side comparison of antibody responses in mice administered intranasal emricasan with those in mice administered recombinant IL-1alpha (rIL-1alpha). The results showed that the levels of OVA-specific serum IgG1 and BALF IgA induced by emricasan were comparable to those induced by rIL-1alpha (Fig. 5C, D). However, the results also showed that OVA-specific IgE production, which was significantly upregulated in the group of mice administered rIL-1alpha, was not significantly induced in the group that received emricasan (Fig. 5E). Because TNF was upregulated in AMs in response to emricasan (Fig. S2A), we therefore wondered whether emricasan-induced TNF production contributes to the regulation of an isotype shift toward IgE. To confirm the effect of TNF on the isotype shift, we compared the antibody responses of mice that received rIL-1alpha intranasally with or without recombinant TNF (rTNF). The results showed that co-administration of rIL-1alpha and rTNF was more effective in upregulating OVA-specific serum IgG1 and BALF IgA than rIL-1alpha alone, but did not significantly change OVA-specific serum IgE (Fig. 5F-H). Furthermore, we observed that the ratios of IgG1/IgE and IgA/IgE were significantly upregulated by the co-administration of rIL-1alpha with rTNF compared with rIL-1alpha alone (Fig. 5I, J). These findings may explain the role of TNF in regulating the isotype shift toward IgE. These results also suggest that emricasan is a potent candidate pulmonary mucosal vaccine adjuvant, promoting antigen-specific IgA in the airway mucosa and systemic IgG via RIPK1/RIPK3-mediated necroptosis of AMs in the lung, while reducing IgE production and inducing no ICD except in AMs. Finally, we conducted an immunization model using the human-applicable type A influenza virus strain H1N1 A/California/07/09 HA antigen to assess the efficacy of emricasan as a mucosal adjuvant. The results demonstrated that the intranasal administration of HA antigen with emricasan significantly increased HA-specific serum IgG1 and BALF IgA titers compared with administration of HA antigen alone (Fig. S10). Collectively, these findings indicate that emricasan functions as an intranasal mucosal adjuvant, stimulating systemic IgG and mucosal IgA production and thereby potentially enhancing host defense against respiratory pathogens such as influenza virus.

passages.text: Discussion

Necroptosis is a type of programmed (or regulated) cell death that is thought to function as an early defense mechanism against viral infections. Although the importance of rapid inflammatory responses during the early phase of infection, particularly in airway immune defense, has been demonstrated in many studies, no reports have yet directly demonstrated the relationship between necroptosis and the induction of adaptive immune responses, such as IgA production. We have now demonstrated that RIPK1/RIPK3-mediated necroptosis is associated with antigen-specific IgG and IgA antibody responses.

To begin with, we found that in AMs, cell death was specifically induced by pan-caspase inhibitors without any additional necroptosis triggers such as TNF or SMAC mimetics compounds targeting cellular inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (cIAPs) or X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis protein (XIAP)s. We further demonstrated that caspase-8, an apoptosis initiator that regulates necroptosis and pyroptosis and is involved in the differentiation and function of macrophages, is expressed as a mature form under steady-state condition in AMs. Furthermore, in AMs, robust induction of necroptosis and IL-1alpha production required the inhibition of multiple caspases, including caspase-1, -3, -7, and -8. Based on these results, we raised a new pharmacological and biological question regarding the induction of necroptosis, although the detailed mechanisms remain to be clarified. In addition, we demonstrated that the cell death induced by pan-caspase inhibitors was almost entirely dependent on RIPK1/RIPK3-mediated necroptosis, which is generally associated with signaling downstream of TNFRs or related death-domain-containing receptors. However, we ruled out the involvement of the TNF-TNFR signaling axis in this process, and the precise upstream mechanisms also remain under investigation.

Next, we demonstrated that IL-1alpha release after induction of RIPK1/RIPK3-mediated necroptosis is responsible for the induction of antibody responses because mice lacking IL-1R1 had severely inhibited antibody responses. In fact, some studies have already shown that recombinant IL-1alpha has the potential to be an intranasal mucosal adjuvant; however, we observed characteristic differences in antibody responses, such as IgE production, when comparing recombinant IL-1alpha and emricasan. Hence, we speculate that, in addition to IL-1alpha, other signaling pathway such as death receptor-related signaling may also contribute to necroptosis-dependent antibody responses. We also found that emricasan stimulate AMs to release TNF. Previous studies reporting serological analysis of inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis patients who received infliximab, an anti-TNF drug, suggested that infliximab attenuates the immunogenicity of vaccines in these patients. In addition, in a mouse model of intranasal vaccination, co-administration of antigen with a highly bioactive modified recombinant TNF significantly upregulated both systemic and mucosal immune responses. These studies indicated the immunogenicity of TNF for vaccinations. Our findings revealed that TNF contributes to isotype switching, suggesting that TNF may serve as a key factor in modulating the IgE response by emricasan.

No nasal adjuvants are approved for use in humans, and therefore we are interested in exploring and developing effective and clinically acceptable pulmonary mucosal adjuvants. In this study, we selected emricasan from a large number of caspase inhibitors because of its effectiveness and advantages for human use. Emricasan, developed by Idun Pharmaceutical, is an irreversible pan-caspase inhibitor is currently under investigation for the treatment of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), a condition characterized by extensive hepatocyte apoptosis. Unfortunately, emricasan failed to reach the primary endpoints in a Phase 2 clinical trial, possibly due to its induction of an alternative, proinflammatory form of cell death it induced. However, emricasan is well tolerated and was successful in a Phase 1 clinical trial, suggesting that it may be safe and less toxic than other candidate molecules, such as toxins; however, its use is currently limited to oral administration. In addition, we observed that emricasan induces robust antigen-specific serum IgG1 and BALF IgA without significantly inducing antigen-specific serum IgE, which is responsible for type 1 allergic hypersensitivity; this may explain the reduced incidence of post-injection side effects.

We conclude that necroptosis, a type of programmed cell death, is a biological mechanism for inducing optimal immunity that may be a promising target for the development of pulmonary mucosal vaccine adjuvants for inducing lung IgA. The caspase inhibitor emricasan may be a candidate molecule whose adjuvanticity is almost entirely dependent on RIPK1/RIPK3-mediated necroptosis.

passages.text: Intensified pegylated-asparaginase in consolidation therapy improved outcome of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for adult T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia

Research on the optimal consolidation therapy for adult T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) remains limited, and how to integrate pediatric-inspired chemotherapy with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (SCT) is less addressed. Based on retrospective analysis indicating that 4 doses of pegylated-asparaginase (PEG-Asp) prior to SCT were optimal for survival, we designed a PEG-Asp-intensified pediatric-inspired regimen, PDT-ALL-2016, for adult T-ALL (NCT03564704). In this protocol, SCT administered following 4 or 5 doses of PEG-Asp. The impact of PEG-Asp on transplantation outcomes was evaluated in two cohorts: the prospective PDT-ALL-2016 cohort (2016.1-2021.12, N = 63) and the retrospective adult regimen cohort (2008.1-2015.12, N = 61). With intensified PEG-Asp consolidation, the prospective cohort exhibited superior survival compared to the retrospective cohort. Furthermore, within the prospective cohort, patients who received non-truncated PEG-Asp demonstrated better survival than those who received a truncated dose. Then, the entire cohort was stratified into high-dose (4-5 doses, N = 45), medium-dose (2-3 doses; N = 33) and low-dose (0-1 doses; N = 46) groups, based on the number of PEG-Asp doses administrated pre-SCT. The high-dose group showed superior survival compared to the other two groups in both the entire cohort and in subgroup analysis. Our findings indicate that high-dose PEG-Asp is associated with improved outcome in adult T-ALL undergoing SCT.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00277-025-06576-8.
Introduction

T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) accounts for approximately 20-25% of adult ALL cases. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (SCT) has long been considered the cornerstone of treatment for adult ALL when treated with standard adult protocols. However, the introduction of pediatric-inspired regimens has significantly improved survival rates for adult T-ALL. Both allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and pediatric-inspired chemotherapy regimens can reduce the relapse rate of adult ALL to approximately 40%. Nevertheless, the optimal integration of SCT with pediatric-inspired chemotherapy in T-ALL to further improve survival remains underexplored.

Depletion of asparagine by administration of the asparaginase (Asp) has been a critical component of the pediatric-inspired regimen. We retrospectively observed that post-SCT survival in adult ALL was associated with the cumulative dose of pegylated-asparaginase (PEG-Asp), with 4 doses demonstrating the best survival. Based on this findings, we designed PDT-ALL-2016 pediatric-inspired protocol (NCT03564704), in which SCT is performed after patients receive four or five doses of PEG-Asp during chemotherapy.
In this study, we demonstrate that high-dose PEG-Asp administration prior to SCT significantly improves survival, effectively combining SCT with pediatric-inspired regimen for adult T-ALL patients.
Methods
Patients and pre-HSCT chemotherapy

This study enrolled 124 consecutive subjects diagnosed with T-ALL who underwent HSCT from 2008.1 to 2021.12, with outcomes updated in 2023.1. Data were collected retrospectively for patients managed between 2008.1 and 2015.12 in adult cohort, and prospectively during 2016.1 to 2021.12 in PDT-ALL-2016 cohort. Informed consent was obtained from all the patients. This study was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Board of Nanfang Hospital, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

The retrospective cohort included patients before 2015.12. In this cohort, patients were treated with adult protocol, including VDLP (Vincristine, Daunorubicin or Idarubicin, PEG-Asp, and Prednisone) or VIP (Vincristine, Daunorubicin or Idarubicin, and Prednisone) as an induction therapy, followed by 3 cycles of Hyper-CVAD A/B consolidation and subsequent SCT. Variable doses of PEG-Asp was added into the consolidation, according to doctors' decision and donors' preparation.

The prospective PDT-ALL-2016 protocol was used from 2016.1, this protocol had been previously reported. SCT was recommended for all patients diagnosed with T-ALL. The timing of SCT was scheduled after 2 phases and 3 blocks of PEG-Asp-containing induction and consolidation therapies (total of 4 or 5 doses PEG-Asp was administrated pre-SCT), the detailed protocol was attached in the supplemental data. We uniformly employ the long-acting PEG-Asp as first-line treatment to reduce the risk of allergic reactions, improve patient compliance, and maximize the total PEG-Asp dosage. We utilize a Tolerated Dosage (TD-Asp) titration approach: the initial dose starts at 2000 U/m2. If the recovery time from coagulation disorders exceeds two weeks, the subsequent dose is reduced by 20%. This process is repeated iteratively until the dose at which coagulation disorders resolve within two weeks is identified as the tolerated dose. Additionally, the maximum single dose of asparaginase for any individual is capped at 3750 IU/m2.

The risk classification in this study was reported previously. High-risk features included: (1) white blood cell count (WBC) count >= 100 x 109/L; (2) complex karyotype (3) T-cell precursor (ETP) immunophenotype; (4) central nervous system leukemia (CNSL) at diagnosis.

CR was defined as disappearance of leukemic blasts in the peripheral blood and < 5% blasts in the bone marrow (BM) aspirate, recovery of blood cell count, and lack of extramedullary disease. MRD evaluation took place prior to consolidation (day 45) and before SCT. MRD assessment was determined by 8-color flow cytometry according to the standardized EuroFlow methodology as previously described, cutoff values of MRD-positive were defined as 0.01%. bone marrow samples were used for the monitoring of MRD.
Transplant modalities

Patients received SCT from human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched sibling donor (MSD), unrelated-donor (MUD) or haploidentical related donor (HID). Donor selection was based on patients' biological characteristics and patients or guardians consent. TBI/Cy (total body irradiation: 4.5 Gy/d on days - 5 and - 4 from a linear accelerator with lung and lens shielding, cyclophosphamide: 60 mg/kg once daily on days - 3 to - 2) was the conditioning regimens as previously reported. Acute and chronic graft-versus-host diseases (GVHD) were diagnosed and graded according to previously reported criteria. Cyclosporine A (CsA) combined with methotrexate (MTX) were used for GVHD prophylaxis in patients with MSD transplant. CsA + MTX + antithymocyte globulin and mycophenolate were used in patients undergoing MUD or HID SCT.
Statistical methods

Associations between categorical variables were assessed by a Fisher exact test, while the Wilcoxon two sample test was performed to test for differences between continuous variables. Overall survival (OS) was measured from the date of transplantation to the date of death or last follow-up. Leukemia-free survival (LFS) was measured from the date of transplantation to the date of event occurred or at the last follow-up. Relapse or death by any cause were considered as events in the LFS analysis. Cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR) was calculated from the date of transplantation to the date of relapse, considering non-relapse mortality (NRM) as a competing event. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to compare survival. Probabilities of NRM and CIR were generated using cumulative incidence estimates to account for competing risks and compared by Gray's test. To adjust for differences in baseline characteristics, Cox proportional hazards regression was used.
The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author (hanson_tcm@126.com) upon reasonable request.
Results
Patients' characteristics

A total of 124 adult T-ALL patients who underwent SCT were enrolled in this study. Among them, 61 patients were from the retrospective adult protocol cohort, and 63 were from the prospective PDT-ALL-2016 cohort (Fig. 1). The baseline characteristics of both cohorts are summarized in Table 1, with no significant differences observed between the two groups.

Effect of pretransplant PEG-Asp dose for survival in retrospective cohort and prospective cohort

Based on retrospective observation, we found that clinical outcomes for adult ALL (both B and T-ALL) improved with increasing doses of PEG-Asp administered during pre-SCT consolidation. A trend toward the best survival was observed with 4 doses of PEG-Asp, compared to lower doses (Figure S1). In 2016, we designed the PDT-ALL-2016 protocol, in which SCT was performed following 2 phases and 3 blocks of PEG-Asp-containing induction and consolidation therapies (the use of PEG-Asp in phase 2 induction was determined by MRD response and risk classification).

Survival for prospective cohort versus retrospective cohort, and effective of full dose PEG-Asp in prospective cohort. (A) Overall survival (OS), (B) leukemia-free survival (LFS), (C) cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR) and (D) non-relapse mortality (NRM) for prospective PDT-ALL-2016 cohort versus retrospective adult regimen cohort. (E) OS and (LFS) for non-truncated (4-5 doses) versus truncated (0-3 doses) PEG-Asp dose group in prospective PDT-ALL-2016 cohort

In T-ALL, intensified PEG-Asp treatment in the prospective cohort resulted in superior survival outcomes compared to the retrospective cohort. A significantly higher proportion of patients in the prospective cohort achieved MRD-negative status prior to transplantation (74.6% vs. 62.5%, Table 1). The 5-year OS rates was 69.3% (58.1-82.6%) in the prospective cohort, versus 46.3% (35.1-61.1%) in the retrospective cohort (p =.001). The 5-year LFS rates was 61.8% (55.0-69.4%) versus 39.0% (33.5-45.3%) (p =.001), in prospective and retrospective cohorts, respectively (Fig. 2AB). The 5-year CIR was 17.1% (8.5-28.1%) vs. 42.3% (29.2-57.1%), and the NRM had no statistical difference between two cohorts (Fig. 2CD).
Effect of intensified versus truncated PEG-Asp dose prior to SCT in PDT-ALL-2016 cohort

To assess the effect of intensified PEG-Asp administration in the PDT-ALL-2016 prospective cohort, we compared survival outcomes between patients who received 4 or 5 full doses of PEG-Asp (non-truncated) and those who received truncated doses due to intolerable toxicity. In the PDT-ALL-2016 cohort, high-dose PEG-Asp still showed better survival. The 5-year OS was 78.2% (66.-91.9%) in the non-truncated dose group, compared to 52.1% (33.2-81.6%) in the truncated dose group. The 5-year LFS was 78.2% (66.5-91.9%) in the non-truncated dose group, compared to 25.1% (25.1-72.9%) in the truncated dose group (Fig. 2 EF).

passages.text: Outcome of high-dose PEG-Asp versus medium- and low-dose in entire cohort

To further assess the impact of high-dose PEG-Asp on survival, we analyzed outcomes across the entire T-ALL cohort. The OS and LFS were superior in 4-5 doses PEG-Asp group (N = 45; 36.2%; high-dose group), followed by the 3, 2, 1 and 0 doses group (Figure S2), survival were similar between 2 and 3 doses (N = 33;26.6%; defined as medium-dose), and 0-1 dose (N = 46; 37.2%; defined as low-dose). Patient characteristics in the three groups are summarized in Table 1, with baseline characteristics balanced across groups.

The clinical outcomes were superior in high-dose group (Fig. 3). The 5-year OS rates were 79.2% (67.9-92.3%) for high-dose group, 63.4% (48.9-83.2%) for the medium-dose group, and 35.3% (23.6-52.8%) for the low-dose group (p <.001). The 5-year LFS were 68.2% (53.3-87.2%) for the high-dose group, 50.3% (34.3-73.8%) for the medium-dose group, and 26.0% (16.0-42.4%) for the low-dose group (p <.001). The 5-year CIR was 13.4% (3.3-30.7%) for the high-dose group, 40.5% (21.3-59.0%) for the medium-dose group, and 58.0% (42.8-71.6%) for the low-dose group (p <.001; Fig. 3 C). The 5-year NRM were similar across the three groups, with rates of 18.5% (8.5-31.5%), 9.1% (2.3-21.9%), and 15.2% (6.6-27.2%) for the high-, medium-, and low-dose groups, respectively (p =.514; Fig. 3D).
Toxicity

passages.text: Table S1 and Table S2 shows the induction and consolidation cycles related toxicities according to adult regimen cohort versus PDT-ALL-2016 cohort, or low-, medium- and high-dose groups. Infections were the most common toxicities. During the induction therapy, grade 3 to 4 infections occurred in 31 (50.8%) patients in the adult regimen cohort and 30 (47.6%) in the PDT-ALL-2016 cohort, while elevated amylase/lipase (any grade) was observed in 4 (6.6%) and 7 (11.1%) patients, respectively. Acute pancreatitis developed in 2 (3.3%) and 2 (3.2%) cases across the two cohorts. During the consolidation therapy phase, grade 3 to 4 infections were observed in 38 (62.3%) patients in the adult regimen cohort and 36 (57.1%) in the PDT-ALL-2016 cohort. Pancreatic enzyme elevation (any grade) occurred in 3 (4.9%) and 9 (14.3%) patients, respectively. Acute pancreatitis was documented in 3 (4.9%) patients receiving the adult regimen, whereas no cases were reported in the PDT-ALL-2016 cohort.

To further investigate the role of high-dose PEG-Asp pretransplant, subgroup analysis were conducted. As shown in Fig. 4 and Table S3. High-dose PEG-Asp showed superior survival in all subsets, except pre-SCT MRD-positive subset. For ETP ALL, the 5-year OS was 79.2% (67.9-92.3%), 63.4% (48.9-82.3%) and 35.3% (23.6-52.8%) in high-, medium-, and low-dose groups, respectively. The 5-year OS of non-ETP T-ALL was 82.6% (68.4-99.6%), 65.0% (47.1-89.6%), and 37.7% (23.7-59.8%), respectively. Of note, in MRD-negative subsets, high-dose PEG-Asp was also associated with better 5-year OS and lower relapse rates. The 5-year OS was 85.2% (74.0-98.1%), 68.1% (51.2-90.7%), 51.6% (33.2-80.4%) in high-, medium-, and low-dose groups, respectively.

In multivariate analysis of the entire cohort (Table 2), high-dose PEG-Asp was identified as a protective factor for OS (HR = 0.27, 0.10-0.73, p =.011), LFS (HR = 0.16, 0.06-0.46, p =.001) and CIR (HR = 0.03, 0.01-0.17, p =.001)), and did not influence NRM (p =.331). Meanwhile, the positive pre-SCT MRD negatively influenced survival (Table 2).
Discussion

For adult T-ALL, SCT remains the most effective anti-leukemic therapy, reducing relapse rates to 30-40%. With the adoption of pediatric-inspired chemotherapy, the survival of adult T-ALL has improved significantly, achieving relapse rates comparable to those observed in patients undergoing allo-HSCT. However, how to combine SCT and pediatric-inspired regimen to further improve survival for adult T-ALL is less addressed. Herein, we showed that presented that intensified PEG-Asp administration prior to SCT is strongly associated with improved outcomes.

Depletion of asparagine through Asp is a key component of chemotherapy for ALL, and its significance has been well established in pediatric T-ALL. In adult T-ALL, several studies have demonstrated that pediatric-inspired regimens containing L-Asp are associated with superior survival outcomes. Notably, PEG-Asp has shown enhanced anti-leukemic effects compared to the native enzyme. However, research on the optimal consolidation therapy for adult T-ALL remains limited. Previous study had demonstrated that exposure to L-Asp longer than 20 weeks showed improved outcomes compared with shorter exposure. Therefore, in PDT-ALL-2016 protocol, SCT was scheduled after the administration of 4 to 5 doses of PEG-Asp.

Relapse after SCT is the primary cause of treatment failure in ALL. Many studies have confirmed that MRD status prior to SCT is the most powerful predictor of survival in adult ALL. Most MRD turning positive occurs within the first 3 months post-SCT, and relapse manifest within 9 months after HSCT. This time window coincident with time required for immune reconstitution to exert graft versus leukemia (GVL) effect (3 months for cellular immunity, and 12 months for full immune reconstitution). The PDT-ALL-2016 protocol emphasizes the optimization of pre-SCT chemotherapy through intensified PEG-Asp-containing consolidation to achieve deep remission as far as possible, prevent early relapse, and allow sufficient time for immune system reconstitution to fully exert the GVL effect.

The critical role of PEG-Asp as a cornerstone of pediatric-inspired regimens has been extensively studied. However, the optimal pre-transplant doses of PEG-Asp remains controversial for patients undergoing SCT. This study therefore focuses on investigating the quantitative optimization of PEG-Asp administration prior to transplantation. In this study, intensified PEG-Asp consolidation led to a higher proportion of patients achieving MRD negativity prior to SCT, which may partially explain the improved survival in prospective cohort and high-dose PEG-Asp group. In fact, for those who achieved MRD-negative status, more sensitive techniques, such as next-generation sequencing-based MRD, may detect residual leukemic cells. We speculate that intensified PEG-Asp administration not only increased the proportion of patients achieving MRD negativity before SCT but also achieved a deeper MRD response. This hypothesis is supported by subgroup analysis, which demonstrated that in the MRD-negative pre-SCT subset, the high-dose PEG-Asp group exhibited superior OS, LFS, and CIR compared to the medium-dose and low-dose groups. Our previous study, the PASS-ALL trial, suggested that the PDT-ALL-2016 protocol may induce durable or deeper MRD responses (d/d MRD) in HR-ALL. In that study, as consolidation treatment, PDT-ALL-2016 regimen resulted in significant longer time-to-positive MRD than adult protocol.

We compared toxicities between the two cohorts during both induction and consolidation phases. The results demonstrated that high-dose PEG-Asp exhibited an overall manageable safety profile. Consistent with most regimens, infections and elevated liver enzymes remained the most common adverse events. However, the reported incidence of PEG-Asp-specific toxicities, such as pancreatitis and thrombosis, varies significantly across studies. In our cohort, these toxicities occurred at relatively low and controllable rates. It is particularly noteworthy that adverse events such as elevated pancreatic enzymes, thrombosis, and pancreatitis may lead to the withholding of PEG-Asp during the corresponding chemotherapy block. Consequently, the incidence of such adverse events in the high-dose group was 0.

passages.text: Limitations of this study include the extended time interval between the adult regimen cohort (2008-2015) and the PDT-ALL-2016 pediatric-inspired cohort (2016-2022). The evolution of transplantation modality (e.g., increasing use of haploidentical donors) during this period may have introduced confounding bias in inter-cohort comparisons. To address this, we incorporated transplantation modality as a covariate in multivariate analysis, which confirmed high-dose PEG-Asp as an independent prognostic factor. An additional consideration is that the high-dose PEG-Asp group predominantly comprised patients from the PDT-ALL-2016 cohort, whereas medium/low-dose groups were derived from the adult regimen and PDT-ALL-2016 cohorts. Consequently, the superior survival observed with high-dose therapy could theoretically be attributed to protocol differences rather than PEG-Asp dose itself. To mitigate this confounding effect and isolate the therapeutic impact of high-dose PEG-Asp, we performed an intra-cohort comparison within the PDT-ALL-2016 cohort, evaluating outcomes between patients receiving full 4 to 5 doses versus those administered 0 to 3 doses. This analysis demonstrated significantly improved survival among patients complete high-dose PEG-Asp therapy, thereby substantiating its efficacy while minimizing cohort-derived bias.

In summary, our study demonstrates that in adult T-ALL patients undergoing transplantation, adequate consolidation therapy (three cycles) and sufficient asparaginase exposure prior to transplantation are essential. High-dose asparaginase (four doses) reduces post-transplant relapse rates, exhibits manageable toxicity, and does not increase NRM, thereby enabling more patients to achieve superior long-term survival. Furthermore, our subgroup analysis revealed that even among patients who achieved pre-transplant MRD negativity, those receiving high-dose asparaginase had better survival outcomes compared to those with lower asparaginase exposure. This suggests that high-dose asparaginase may induce deeper and more durable MRD responses.
