passages.text: The sulfur mobilization step of the SUF pathway begins with a pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme, SufS, which catalyzes the desulfurization of L-Cys. This reaction yields a persulfide on a catalytic Cys residue and L-Ala as a byproduct. SufS utilizes a sulfur transferase, either SufU or SufE, depending on the organism, to transfer sulfur downstream within the SUF pathway for Fe S cluster assembly. Extended X-ray Absorption Fine Structure (EXAFS) spectra indicated that the Zn2+ site in B. subtilis SufU (BsSufU) is coordinated by three S atoms (2.3 A) and one O atom (2.0 A). These results are in consistent with both the NMR structure of BsSufU and the crystal structure of the SufU from Mycoplasma penetrans (Mpe) (PDB: 2AZH and 8ZTQ, respectively), both of which reveal a tetrahedral Cys3Asp coordination environment for Zn2+ (Cys66, Cys41, Cys128, and Asp43). Despite these data, the coordination number of the Zn2+ center remains disputed, as additionally published NMR and X-ray crystallography structures of BsSufU uniquely reveal bidentate coordination of the Asp residue (PDB: 1XJS and 6JZV). Hudspeth et al. showed that, like BsSufU, S. aureus SufU (SaSufU) coordinates one Zn2+ ion, and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) revealed that SaSufU exhibits a similar fold to BsSufU. However, SaSufU was shown not to stimulate SaSufS to the same degree that BsSufU stimulates BsSufS. This suggests possible mechanistic, structural, or functional differences for SaSufU.

In B. subtilis, a Zn2+-ligand swapping mechanism for sulfur transfer from BsSufS to BsSufU was proposed based on the X-ray crystal structure of the BsSufU-BsSufS complex (Fig. 1). This structure revealed that His342 in BsSufS displaces a BsSufU Zn2+ ligand, Cys41, resulting in a Cys2HisAsp coordination environment for the Zn2+ ion. This displacement allows Cys41 of BsSufU direct access to the otherwise buried active site of BsSufS, thereby permitting persulfide transfer to BsSufU. A similar ligand-swapping mechanism was recently proposed based on the X-ray structure for the SufS-SufU complex from Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), which involves His354 of MtbSufS. Using a His342Tyr variant, Fujishiro et al. additionally demonstrated that His342 of BsSufS is critical for the activation of BsSufS cysteine desulfurase activity by BsSufU, and Ma et al. utilized site-directed mutagenesis of Gln342, the proposed Zn2+-ligating residue in MpeSufS, to demonstrate that it influences both the catalytic activation and complex affinity of MpeSufS-SufU. Despite these data, no solution evidence for the proposed ligand swapping mechanism for a SufS-SufU complex has been reported to date, which is a critical step in establishing whether such a mechanism can occur in vivo.

Herein, the Zn2+-ligand swapping mechanism was investigated in SaSufU, which shares ~70 % sequence homology with BsSufS. Given the absence of X-ray crystallographic data for SaSufU, the Zn2+ ion was substituted with the catalytically competent Co2+ ion providing a spectroscopically active  system allowing the active site to be examined directly via electronic absorption (UV-Vis) and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopies. EXAFS data for both the Zn2+- and Co2+-bound forms were also recorded, providing in-solution structural information regarding both resting state SaSufU, as well as the SaSufS-SaSufU complex. Additionally, SaSufS mutants lacking the histidine residue required for ligand exchange (His349) were shown to bind Zn2+-SaSufU but were not activated. The combination of these data provides in-solution evidence for a persulfide transfer mechanism from SaSufS to SaSufU.
Materials and methods
Materials

All chemicals were purchased from commercial sources, Ambeed, Amresco, Fisher, Oakwood, or Sigma-Aldrich, unless stated otherwise, and were of the highest quality available. The SaSufS and SaSufU plasmids were purchased from Genscript. BL-21(DE3) cells, kanamycin, Luria-Bertani (LB) Broth, nitric acid (trace metal grade), imidazole, sodium chloride (NaCl), and tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane hydrochloride (Tris-HCl) were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Isopropyl-beta-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG), potassium chloride (KCl), L-cysteine, L-alanine, trichloroacetic acid (TCA), boric acid, Chelex 100, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), sodium hydroxide, potassium cyanide, hydrochloric acid, and glycerol were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), 3-morpholnopropane-1-sulfonic acid (MOPS), dithiothreitol, 1,10-phenanthroline, tris (2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), and 2,3-napthalenedicarboxyaldehyde (NDA) were purchased from Ambeed. Ethanol was purchased from Pharmco. Cobalt chloride hexahydrate was purchased from Amresco. Immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) nickel nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) purification columns (5 mL) were purchased from Qiagen, and gel filtration standards were purchased from General Electric Healthcare.
Plasmids, cell cultures, and protein purification

Plasmids (pET-28a(+)) containing tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease-cleavable N-terminal histidine tagged (His6) genes corresponding to SaSufS and SaSufU were purchased from Genscript (Piscataway, NJ) using the same SaSufU and SaSufS nucleotide sequences found in plasmids described in previous work. All plasmids were transformed into BL-21(DE3) E. coli cells in the presence of kanamycin at a final concentration of 50 mug/mL. Cells were grown in 800 mL of LB broth containing 50 mug/mL of kanamycin at 37  C until an OD600 of 0.8-1 was reached. Recombinant protein expression was induced via addition of 0.2 mM IPTG, and cells were grown for an additional 20 h at 20  C. Upon induction, cells recombinantly expressing SaSufS only were supplemented with 934 muM PLP.

Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 9000 xg for 15 min. Cell pellets were resuspended and lysed in binding buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 500 mM KCl, 20 mM imidazole) and centrifuged at 32,000 xg at 4  C for 55 min. The supernatant was filtered through a 0.45 mum nitrocellulose syringe filter before loading onto an IMAC Ni-NTA column. After washing the column with at least five column volumes of the binding buffer, the protein was eluted with a 60 mL linear gradient to 100 % elution buffer (50 mM Tris- HCl, pH 7.8, 500 mM KCl, 250 mM imidazole). Fractions were collected, concentrated, and buffer exchanged three times into assay storage buffer (100 mM MOPS, pH 8.0, 10 % glycerol) using Amicon Ultra-15 Centrifugal filters (30 kDa cutoff for SaSufS and 10 kDa cutoff for SaSufU) and an Eppendorf 5810 R centrifuge by spinning at 3000 xg until the sample volume was less than 1 mL. SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) revealed single polypeptide bands at ~48 kDa for SaSufS and ~ 19 kDa for SaSufU, consistent with previous studies. Purified protein was aliquoted, flash-frozen, and stored at -80  C.

His6-tagged TEV protease was expressed and purified as described in previous work. His6 tags were cleaved from SaSufS and SaSufU by incubating purified SaSufS or SaSufU with TEV protease in a 1:5 ratio of TEV protease: SufS or SufU for 24 h at 4  C in 50 mM Tris buffer containing 1.5 mM TCEP, 20 % glycerol, 0.5 mM EDTA, at pH 7.5. His tag-cleaved SaSufS or SaSufU was purified from TEV protease on an IMAC Ni-NTA column via elution with binding buffer. Recovered protein was concentrated, and buffer exchanged into the assay storage buffer (100 mM MOPS, pH 8.0, 10 % glycerol).

The metal content of as-purified SaSufU was determined via inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES). SaSufU was digested in 58 % trace metal grade nitric acid for at least 24 h. before samples were diluted to 10 mL with nanopure water. Digested samples were passed through a 0.2 mum filter to remove any particulate before ICP-AES analysis.
Site-directed mutagenesis

Site-directed mutants of the SaSufS residue His349 was performed using an Agilent QuikChange Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit. Briefly, SaSufS-TEV-His6 plasmid extracted from NEB-turbo E. coli cells using a Promega Wizard Plus SV Miniprep kit were amplified with the following primers (purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies), each containing altered bases corresponding to either an His349Ala or His349Phe SaSufS mutant.
His349Ala forward: 5'-GTTCATCCGGCTGATGTGGCGACCGCCGTG-3'
His349Ala reverse: 5'-CACATCAGCCGGATGAACATCTTGCAAATTAAACG-3'
His349Phe forward: 5'-GTTCATCCGTTTGATGTGGCGACCGCCGTG-3'
His349Phe reverse: 5'- GCCACATCAAACGGATGAACATCTTGCAAATTAAACG-3'

Mutant plasmids were transformed into NEB-turbo cells, and single colonies expressing kanamycin resistance were selected, grown, and stored at -70  C in 15 % glycerol (v/v). Plasmid extracted from these cells was transformed into BL-21(DE3) E. coli cells for expression of mutant protein, and mutagenesis was confirmed via whole plasmid sequencing (Azenta). All variant proteins were expressed, purified, His6-tag cleaved, and stored in the same manner as that described for WT SaSufS.
Metal removal and Co2+ substitution

Prior to metal removal of SaSufU, all buffers were prepared in acid-washed glassware to remove trace metals. Nanopure water (2 L) was treated with 50 g Chelex 100 for 4 h with stirring, followed by filtering using a Nalgene Rapid-Flow Sterile Bottle Top under vacuum. To avoid the formation of disulfide bonds in the cysteine-rich active site of apo-SaSufU, all incubations and buffer exchanges were performed in a Coy anaerobic chamber maintained at 1.5 % hydrogen and < 40 ppm oxygen, and all metal removal buffers were degassed and incubated in the Coy Chamber for 12 h. prior to their use. Zn2+-supplemented SaSufU was first anaerobically transferred to an Amicon 10 kDa Ultra-15 Centrifugal filter and diluted to 15 mL with 25 mM MOPS at pH 8, 10 mM KCl, 10 % ethanol, 10 mM 1,10-phenanthroline, and 2 mM DTT (Buffer B). The protein was incubated for 2 h at room temperature before it was concentrated to ~1 mL via centrifugation. This incubation process was repeated 4 times, followed by 4 buffer exchanges (performed using the same filter) into Chelex-treated 25 mM MOPS buffer, pH 8, containing 10 mM KCl (Buffer A). SaSufU was confirmed to be apo via ICP-AES analysis.

Preparation of the Co2+-substituted SaSufU was accomplished by the addition of CoCl2 6H2O dissolved in water containing 10 mM KCl. A single equivalent of Co2+was added to apo-SaSufU in Chelex 100-treated 25 mM MOPS buffer, pH 8, containing 10 mM KCl, and the sample was mixed until any precipitate disappeared. The concentrated sample was a light blue colour. Apo-SaSufU and Co-substituted SaSufU were both stored at -70  C.
Cysteine desulfurase assay

Cysteine desulfurase activity was determined using a 96-well plate using a procedure adapted Addo et al. Briefly, alanine production was quantified using a developing reaction containing napthalene-2,3-dicarboxaldehyde (NDA), which forms a fluorescent adduct with alanine. All assays were prepared using the Eppendorf Xplorer multichannel pipette, a black 96-well plate, and plastic multichannel reservoirs. Reactions (250 muL) comprising 1 muM His6-cleaved SaSufS (WT or His349 mutants), Zn2+-loaded 1 muM SaSufU (with an ICP-AES-confirmed 1 eq. of Zn2+ per monomer), 1 mM L-Cys, and 2 mM TCEP in 25 mM MOPS, pH 8.0, containing 10 mM KCl were initiated in 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes. Where SaSufU was not present, reactions were instead run with 10 muM His6-cleaved SaSufS (WT or His349 mutants). Reactions were quenched after predetermined times with 50 muL of a 10 % TCA solution, which were centrifuged at 21,130 xg for 5-min to remove precipitated protein. Zero time-point reactions were quenched before the addition of Cys and served as zero points to which identically prepared reactions could be normalized. Supernatant (50 muL) was combined with 150 muL of a quenching solution (1.2 mM KCN, 0.12 mM NDA in 127 mM borate, pH 9.0) in a black 96 well plate and allowed to incubate for 1-h before the fluorescence of each was measured (Ex390/Em440) using a BioTek Synergy Neo2 multimode plate reader. For each stated combination of SaSufS and SaSufU, six reactions were prepared and quenched after 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20-min time periods in triplicate, respectively. A six-point standard curve prepared in triplicate and in the same manner as each reaction solution comprising increasing concentrations of L-Ala (0, 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 muM) and correspondingly decreasing concentrations of L-Cys from 1 mM was used to quantify the amount of alanine produced during each reaction based on the observed fluorescence.
Size-exclusion chromatography

Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) was used to determine the degree of complexation, weight, and stoichiometry of the WT Zn2+-SaSufS-SaSufU complex as well as the complexes comprising each His349 SaSufS mutant and Zn2+-SaSufU. A Cytiva Superdex 200 prep grade, 16/600 HiLoad column was calibrated using a 9-point calibration standard curve (0.2 mg/mL blue dextran, 0.2 mg/mL Thyroglobulin, 0.2 mg/mL ferritin, 0.6 mg/mL aldolase, 1.5 mg/mL conalbumin, 2.0 mg/mL ovalbumin, 1.5 mg/mL carbonic anhydrase, 3.0 mg/mL ribonuclease A, 0.8 mg/mL aprotinin). The absorbance at 280 nm of the eluate as a function of volume was fit to the summation of 9 gaussian curves, and the masses of the separated standards were plotted as a function of the volumes at which the corresponding peaks of the curves occurred (SI Fig. 1). WT, His349Ala, or His349Phe SaSufS (400 muM active sites) was combined with 400 muM Zn2+-supplemented SaSufU, and the resulting solution thoroughly mixed. This solution was then manually loaded onto the same column. In all three cases, the absorbance at 280 nm of the resulting eluate was monitored and fit to a single Gaussian curve. This process was repeated with WT SaSufS-Zn2+-SaSufU (50 muM active sites each) in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP, pH 7.8, as well as WT SaSufS-Zn2+-SaSufU (50 muM active sites each) in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.8 following a 1-h incubation in 50 muM Cys at room temperature.
UV-Vis and EPR spectroscopy

UV-Vis spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu UV-2600i spectrophotometer with 1 mL quartz cuvettes between 200 and 900 nm on 150 muM Co2+-SaSufU in 25 mM MOPS, pH 8.0 with 10 mM KCl. To temporally resolve spectra upon timed incubation with cysteine, UV-Vis spectra taken in the presence of cysteine were recorded on an Agilent 8453 UV-Vis spectrophotometer, which contains a diode array. X-band parallel-mode (B0 B1; 9.37 GHz) and perpendicular-mode (B0 B1; 9.63 GHz) EPR spectra were recorded at 10-30 K on an updated Bruker EMX-AA-TDU/L spectrometer equipped with an HP 5350B microwave counter for precise frequency measurement on 1 mM Co2+-SaSufU samples in 25 mM MOPS, pH 8.0 with 10 mM KCl. Cryogenic temperatures were maintained with a ColdEdge/Bruker Stinger S5-L recirculating helium refrigerator, and an Oxford ESR900 cryostat and Mercury ITC temperature controller.
Cobalt titration of SaSufU

Titration of apo-SaSufU with Co2+ was performed via the incremental addition of 18.75 muM CoCl2 6H2O in water containing 10 mM KCl to 1 mL of 150 muM apo-SaSufU in 25 mM MOPS, pH 8.0 with 10 mM KCl. All additions (5 muL of 3.77 mM CoCl2 each) were performed in a 1 mL quartz cuvette. Apo-SaSufU and the CoCl2 solutions were mixed for several seconds until all precipitate disappeared. Before and between each CoCl2 addition, the UV-Vis absorbance spectrum of the Co2+-SaSufU complex was recorded. The overall concentration of CoCl2 in solution was increased in this manner until it reached 3 eq. of SaSufU. The titration was performed in triplicate, and all data were corrected for dilutions resulting from CoCl2 additions.

The d-d transitions at 636 and 735 nm were analyzed for binding stoichiometry (p) and the dissociation constant . Differences in the change in absorbance at both 636 and 735 nm as a function of CoCl2 added were fit to logistic curves to determine the binding stoichiometry of CoCl2. Reported molar absorptivity's were determined based on the per-mole absorbance observed after saturation of the d-d bands, scaled by the difference in the binding stoichiometry from the nearest integer to account for both disulfide-containing and Zn2+ bound SaSufU. X-ray absorption spectroscopy

Samples for X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) were concentrated to at least 1 mM in 25 mM MOPS buffer containing 10 % glycerol to minimize ice crystal diffraction artifacts. Five samples were prepared: Zn2+-SaSufU, Zn2+-SaSufU-SaSufS (1:1 ratio), Co2+-SaSufU, Co2+-SaSufU-SaSufS (1:1 ratio), and Co(II)-SaSufU-SaSufS incubated with 3 mM cysteine for 90 s before freezing in the EXAFS cuvette. The samples were loaded in custom Lucite cuvettes (25 x 3 x 2 mm) sealed with Kapton tape. Zn and Co K-edge near-edge and EXAFS spectra were measured at Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource beamline 7-3, using a Si(220) double-crystal monochromator. The monochromator was detuned to 60 % of maximum to minimize contributions from monochromator harmonics. An Oxford Instruments CF1208 liquid helium cooled cryostat was used to maintain the sample temperature at 7 K. The EXAFS cuvettes were inclined at 45  to the incident X-ray beam to facilitate the measurement of X-ray fluorescence, giving an incident X-ray path length of 2.8 mm. Kalpha12 fluorescence X-rays were measured using a 30-element Ge fluorescence detector (Canberra Industries), fitted with Soller slits and a Cu filter for Zn XAS or an Fe filter for Co XAS (both 3 absorbance) to minimize the relative contribution of scattered radiation. Incident and transmitted X-ray intensities were monitored using nitrogen-filled gas ionization chambers with a sweeping voltage of 1.6 kV. The X-ray energy was calibrated using the first inflection point of a standard Zn or Co foil, measured in transmittance and set as 9660.7 eV or 7709.5 eV, respectively. This was measured at the same time as the sample spectrum using an additional ion chamber positioned downstream of the sample. In-hutch photon shutters were employed to limit the exposure of the sample to the X-ray beam while data were being actively recorded. The K-edge near-edge spectrum was monitored after each scan to ensure the absence of X-ray photochemistry. The radiation dose for each 40 min sweep on beamline 7-3 was estimated to be approximately 77 kGy. At least 8 scans were collected for each sample up to k ~ 17 A-1 with an overall collection time of ~320 min per sample. For the Co samples, a blank sample containing buffer and glycerol was measured as a control. This allowed the subtraction of background signals, in particular the Ge escape peaks inherent to the Ge fluorescence detector.
EXAFS data analysis

EXAFS data were analyzed using the EXAFSPAK suite of programs. Although the samples contained 10 % glycerol as a glassing agent, it was still necessary to examine each individual detector channel for each scan for diffraction effects from ice crystals and to reject the channel if necessary. The same channels were removed for each scan when preparing the spectrum of the buffer blank for subtraction. Curve fitting used the EXAFSPAK program OPT, with single-scattering phase and amplitude functions calculated using FEFF 7.0. The general approach was first to establish the likely backscattering element for each shell (here O/N and S), then assume appropriate initial values for the parameters N, R and sigma2 before floating selected parameters while being cognizant of the likely metal environment and the likelihood of correlated parameters. For example, N and sigma2 can strongly correlate, so it is normal to fix one while floating the other. A single global DeltaE0 was also allowed to float, and the structure was optimized for the best fit. The scale factor used in the fits was 0.90. The fit quality was assessed using the statistical factor  where  EXAFS;  EXAFS. The resolution of the EXAFS measurements was 0.105 A.
Results and discussion
Metal binding and activity

The as-purified SaSufU enzyme routinely contained ~0.6 eq. of Zn2+ based on ICP-AES. As such, purified, His6-cleaved SaSufU was supplemented with 0.5 eq. ZnCl2, and complete Zn2+ occupancy of the supplemented enzyme was confirmed via ICP-AES. Apo-SaSufU was confirmed to be metal-free via ICP-AES analysis after treatment with 1,10-phenanthroline and DTT (only <0.05 eq. of the original Zn2+ was present). Interestingly, initial preps of apo-SaSufU prepared aerobically routinely exhibited an absorption band at ~320 nm despite containing no Zn2+ ions, suggesting the presence of a disulfide bond. Aerobically prepared apo-SaSufU bound significantly less than a full equivalent of Zn2+, suggesting active site obstruction. It was hypothesized, based on the number of cysteines comprising the SaSufU active site that a disulfide bond could form, thereby blocking metal binding. Attempts to reverse disulfide bond formation via DTT or TCEP proved unsuccessful in eliminating the absorption at 320 nm. Therefore, apo-SaSufU was prepared anaerobically, which significantly reduced the absorbance at 320 nm. Anaerobically prepared SaSufU could be reconstituted with nearly its full complement of Co2+ metal ions, confirming the absence of disulfide bonds within the active site of apo-SaSufU.

Anaerobically prepared apo-SaSufU was reconstituted with one eq. of Co2+ resulting in a Co2+-substituted SaSufU enzyme that was lightblue in colour. Cysteine desulfurase activity for WT-SaSufS supplemented with Zn2+-SaSufU or Co2+-SaSufU were determined using Cys as the substrate (Fig. 2A). The observed activity for WT SaSufS was amplified in the presence of both Zn2+-SaSufU and Co2+-SaSufU but not apo-SaSufU, indicating that each metalated SaSufU stimulates SaSufS activity. The addition of Zn2+-SaSufU to SaSufS provided a 10-fold simulation in cysteine desulfurase activity over a reaction time of 20 min, which is significantly greater than previously reported, ~1.5-fold stimulation. The observed increased stimulation is likely due to the removal of the His6 tag, as inclusion of a His6 tag on BsSufU interfered with BsSufS-BsSufU complex formation. Similarly, Co2+-SaSufU exhibited a stimulation factor of ~2-fold compared to the activity of SaSufS with apo-SaSufU, indicating that Co2+-substituted SaSufU can function as a sulfur transfer protein, albeit to a lesser degree than Zn2+-SaSufU. These data are consistent with those previously reported that suggested that Co2+-substituted SufU from other Gram-positive organisms stimulates cysteine desulfurase activity, albeit to a reduced degree compared to Zn2+-SufU.

The X-ray crystal structures of SufS-SufU complexes from more than one organism consistently reveal a SufS2-SufU2 heterotetramer in which a SufU Cys ligand is displaced by a His residue on SufS, termed a ligand swapping mechanism (i.e., achievement of the most energetically-favorable conformation of the SufS-SufU complex appears to necessitate the His-Cys Zn2+ ligand swap proposed to be essential for catalytic activation of SufS). In BsSufS-BsSufU, His342 of BsSufS was shown to displace the Cys41 Zn2+ ligand of BsSufU. To gain insight into the activation of SaSufS cysteine desulfurase activity by SaSufU, the corresponding His residue in SaSufS, His349, was mutated to either an Ala or Phe (His349Ala and His349Phe) neither of which can bind to the active site Zn2+ ion in SaSufU, but the latter of which is capable of pi stacking with the adjacent His347 of SaSufS (SI Figs 3 and 4). Indeed, each mutant exhibited cysteine desulfurase activity like that of WT SaSufS but was not activated by the addition of Zn2+-SaSufU (Fig. 2B), confirming that His349 in SaSufS is crucial for persulfide transfer. That a SaSufS2-SaSufU2 complex forms in solution was confirmed via SEC chromatography, which provided a molecular weight of ~127 kDa for the SaSufS-Zn2+-SaSufU complex, consistent with the expected SaSufS2-SaSufU2 heterotetramer. Pre-incubation of 50 muM SaSufS-Zn2+-SaSufU in 1 eq. Cys for one-hour under non-reducing conditions resulted in no significant change to the SEC chromatogram of the complex, suggesting that Cys does not significantly inhibit SaSufS-Zn2+-SaSufU complex formation at these concentrations. Complex formation for His349 SaSufS mutants in the presence of SaSufU was also investigated via SEC chromatography. A molecular weight of ~127 kDa was observed for both His349 SaSufS mutants, suggesting formation of an SaSufS2-SaSufU2 heterotetramer even though neither His349 SaSufS mutant is capable of ligand swapping (SI Fig. 1). These data indicate that SaSufS-SaSufU complex formation occurs to near completion, independent of His349 and therefore, likely preceding a His-Cys Zn2+ ligand swap.
UV-Vis spectroscopy

Since Co2+-substituted SaSufU can enhance SaSufS activity, albeit to a reduced degree, the Co2+-substituted protein can be used to further examine the proposed Zn2+-ligand swapping mechanism of SaSufS-SaSufU in solution. A 150 muM sample of Co2+-SaSufU was light blue in colour, and the electronic absorption spectrum revealed absorption bands with lambdamax values of 340 nm (epsilon = 2, 760 M-1cm-1), 584 nm (epsilon = 540 M-1cm-1), 636 nm (epsilon = 580 M-1cm-1), and 735 nm (epsilon = 220 M-1cm-1) (Fig. 3). The absorbance at 340 nm is consistent with a S-   Co2+ ligand-to-metal-charge-transfer (LMCT) band, which typically occur between 310 and 340 nm. The observation of a S-   Co2+ LMCT band allows the number of S- ligands bound to the Co2+ ion to be estimated as each bond contributes to the molar absorptivity (epsilon) by 900 to 1200M-1 cm-1. The observed epsilon value at 340 nm for Co2+-SaSufU of 2, 760 M-1cm-1 suggests that three Cys residues coordinate the Co2+ center in Co2+-SaSufU. These data are consistent with the X-ray crystal structure of Zn2+-BsSufU, which revealed a Cys3Asp coordination sphere for the active site Zn2+, and suggest that the SaSufU metal-binding site is similar to that observed in BsSufU.

The remaining absorption bands observed at 584 nm (epsilon = 540 M-1cm-1), 635 nm (epsilon = 580 M-1cm-1), and 735 nm (epsilon = 220 M-1cm-1), were assigned to d-d transitions (Fig. 3; Inset), and provide insight into the nature and number of coordinating ligands. For Co2+ in a tetrahedral coordination environment, intense absorption bands (epsilon > 300M-1 cm-1) are typically observed in the 500 to 750 nm region, while an octahedral coordination geometry provides weak absorption bands with epsilon values typically <= 30M-1 cm-1. As expected, five-coordinate Co2+ centers exhibit epsilon values that are intermediate between octahedral and tetrahedral (50 <= epsilon <= 250M-1 cm-1). The observed d-d absorption bands for Co2+-SaSufU are consistent with a distorted four- or five-coordinate geometry based on their lambdamax values and the observed epsilon values. If five-coordinate, the fifth Co2+ ligand might be the Asp43 ligand coordinating the Co2+ center in a bi-dentate fashion or a water molecule. The former is supported by NMR and X-ray crystal structures of BsSufU (PDB: 1XJS and 6JZV, respectively), in which the Zn2+ center is coordinated by three cysteine residues and an aspartate residue in a bidentate fashion. Similar d-d absorption bands have been observed for Co2+-substituted zinc-finger proteins, which exhibit d-d transitions in the 500-800 nm range with Cys coordination, and those with a Cys3His coordination environment most closely resemble the observed absorption bands for Co2+-SaSufU. Taken together, the UV-Vis data are consistent with a Cys3Asp coordination sphere for Co2+-SaSufU, which is identical to that observed in the Zn2+ center in BsSufU; however, the Co2+ ion in SaSufU may have a fifth weakly bound ligand, resulting in a five-coordinate Co2+ ion.

The observed d-d bands at 636 and 735 nm were utilized for the stepwise addition of Co2+, which yielded titration curves indicating saturation at ~0.8 eq. Co2+ (0.83 +- 0.03 for the 636 nm band and 0.79 +- 0.1 for the 735 nm band), suggesting that a single Co2+ likely binds the SaSufU active site (Fig. 4). Incomplete saturation of apo-SaSufU is likely due to either a small amount of Zn2+-bound SaSufU that was observed after metal removal or disulfide bond formation between active site Cys residues in apo-SaSufU. As such, the titration data were properly scaled with the assumption that only 80 % of the total enzyme active sites were accessible for Co2+ binding. Interestingly, after saturation of the d-d bands was achieved, a new, broad absorption band centered at ~400 nm appeared and reached saturation after an additional ~1 eq. Co2+ was added (SI Fig. 2). This band, which shifted the blue colour of the enzyme to yellow, likely corresponds to adventitious binding of Co2+ to SaSufU. Indeed, a similar absorption band was observed upon addition of 1 eq. of Co2+ to Zn2+-bound SaSufU. Because this band likely does not correspond to active-site saturation of apo-SaSufU with Co2+ but overlaps with the observed absorption bands at 340 and 584 nm, neither of these absorption bands was used for the determination of a Co2+  value. Based on the titration data obtained from the 636 and 735 nm d-d absorption bands, Co2+  values were estimated to be 600 +- 100 nM and 610 +- 80 nM, respectively (Fig. 4). As these data reflect relatively strong Co2+ binding to the SaSufU active site, the observed  values should be viewed an upper limit.

Finally, the UV-Vis spectrum of Co2+-SaSufU was recorded in the presence of SaSufS, since substitution of a Cys ligand in Co2+-SaSufU with a His residue on SaSufS should result in a change in the electronic environment of the Co2+ ion. Surprisingly, upon the addition of 1 eq. of Co2+-SaSufU to 1 eq. of SaSufS, conditions that SEC data confirms the formation a SaSufS2-SaSufU2 heterotetramer, a decrease in the intensity of the S-   Co2+ LMCT band at 340 nm was not observed. Furthermore, only small shifts in the d-d absorption bands of ~5 nm were observed, which would be consistent with complex formation but not displacement of a Cys for a His ligand (Fig. 3). These small changes in the UV-Vis spectrum of Co2+-SaSufU-SaSufS did not significantly change with time, even after incubation for 96 h at 4  C . However, upon the addition of the SaSufS substrate Cys (2 mM) for 15 s, the intensities and lambdamax values of the d-d bands experienced significant deviations. While the 636 nm band exhibited a significant decrease in intensity, the 584 nm was band redshifted, and its intensity increased substantially. The peak of the 735 nm band also redshifted and decreased in intensity. These changes are consistent with those expected for a Cys-His ligand swap, as Co2+-substituted zinc-finger proteins containing a Cys2His2 binding site commonly exhibit d-d bands at 580 and 640 nm, with the 600 nm band exhibiting a strong molar absorptivity of ~900 M-1 cm-1. Interestingly, after 45 s of incubation with 2 mM Cys, the d-d bands expected for resting-state Co2+-SaSufU appeared to partially re-emerge. While a corresponding decrease in the intensity of the 340 nm LMCT band is also expected for a Cys-His ligand exchange, such a change in molar absorptivity is difficult to observe due to significant overlap with the SaSufS PLP absorption. These data suggest that under the conditions used for UV-Vis spectroscopy (i.e. 150 muM active sites), Co2+-SaSufU-SaSufS complexation occurs independently of His-Cys ligand swapping, and the proposed His-Cys Co2+ ligand exchange only occurs in the presence of Cys.
X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS)

The coordination environment for both Zn2+- and Co2+-SaSufU were further examined using X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). In addition to Zn2+- and Co2+-SaSufU bound enzymes, the reaction of Zn2+- and Co2+-SaSufU with SaSufS was also examined where the Co(II)-SaSufU-SaSufS complex was incubated with 3 mM cysteine for 90 s before freezing in the EXAFS cuvette. The normalized Zn and Co K-edge near-edge spectra are presented in Fig. 5. It should be noted that the forms of the Zn near-edge spectra in the left panel is consistent with previously reported four-coordinate Zn2+ with a mixed Zn S and Zn O coordination with only small changes apparent upon binding SaSufS. A small pre-edge feature is observed for all three of the Co2+-SufU samples (arrow in Fig. 5) at 7710.1 eV, which arises from a 1 s   3d transition, which is Laporte-forbidden in centrosymmetric environments (e.g., octahedral), and its intensity is inversely related to coordination number. In this case, the intensity of the observed transition for Co2+-SaSufU is that expected for a five-coordinate Co2+ ion. These data are consistent with the observed electronic absorption spectroscopic data for Co2+-SaSufU. Importantly, the intensity of this band is unchanged for the Co2+-SaSufU-SaSufS complex both before and after the addition of cysteine, implying that the overall coordination number and/or symmetry remains unchanged. Second, there is a clear change in the shape of the near-edge spectrum upon binding SaSufS.
Extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS)

The EXAFS modulations and best-fits for 1 mM samples if Zn-SaSufU and Zn2+-SaSufU:SaSufS together with the corresponding Fourier transform (FT) of the data are provided in Fig. 6 with the best-fit parameters listed in Table 1. It should be noted that the FT data have been phase-corrected, so the peaks occur approximately at the correct distances from the Zn atom. The FT data shows a strong peak at ~2.3 A with a much weaker peak at ~2.0 A. Curve-fitting analysis reveals that these correspond to 3 Zn-S interactions at 2.32 A and a single Zn O interaction at 2.04 A. This corresponds well with the previously reported EXAFS analysis for BsSufU, which revealed 3 S scatters at 2.32 A and 1 N/O scatter at 2.05 A, in accordance with X-ray structure of BsSufU (Cys3Asp). The addition of SaSufS leads to changes in the EXAFS, indicating a structural change at this site. The most straightforward way to analyze this change is to start with the Zn2+-SaSufU fit in Fig. 6(a), fix the Debye-Waller factors, and allow the number of atoms to vary. The result suggests a loss of 0.45 Zn S interactions and a corresponding gain of a similar number of Zn-O/N interactions. This suggests site heterogeneity with a partial ligand exchange of a Zn S ligand with a Zn O or Zn N ligand, consistent with the replacement of Cys by His to form a Cys2AspHis coordination environment. These data suggest partial binding of His349 on SaSufS to the Zn2+ ion in SaSufU under the reaction conditions, consistent with the proposed Zn-ligand swapping mechanism.

Conversely, the EXAFS observed for 1 mM samples of Co2+-SaSufU is, in general, weaker in intensity than the corresponding Zn EXAFS (Figs. 6 and 7a). This result is likely due to either a small amount of Zn2+-bound SaSufU that was observed after metal removal or disulfide bond formation between active site Cys residues in apo-SaSufU. The Co EXAFS has a maximum absolute intensity of  of 4.2 A-3 and FT intensities IFT of 1.3 compared to maxima of  of 5.9 A-3 and IFT of ~2.9 for the Zn data. The Co2+-SaSufU EXAFS (Fig. 7a) comprises two clear shells at ~2.2 A and ~ 1.9 A. Curve-fitting analysis reveals the longer shell is comprised of about 2 Co S interactions at 2.25 A, while the shorter shell is best fit by two Co-O/N interactions at 1.87 A and 2.01 A (Table 1). In view of the likely coordination number of five, as suggested by the near-edge and electronic absorption spectroscopy we investigated whether a third, longer Co S interaction was likely and found that the fit to the data was significantly improved by the inclusion of an additional (N = 0.7) Co S shell at 2.42 A (Table 1). Therefore, the coordination sphere of the Co2+ ion in SaSufU is comprised of 2 Co-O/N ligands, one long distance and one short, and three Co S ligands, with one distance longer than the other two. One rationalization of this fit is that the Co2+ ion is coordinated by the 3 cysteines in the enzyme pocket and one aspartate, with a longer bond to the second oxygen of the Asp ligand as observed in the NMR structure of BsSufU (PDB, 1XJS); however, a water molecule bound to the Co2+ ion cannot be excluded. Even so, the propensity of a high-spin Co2+ ion in a five-coordinate environment to undergo a Jahn Teller distortion might explain the longer Co2+-S and Co2+-O/N bonds as an elongation along the z-axis.

Like the Zn2+-SaSufU EXAFS data, a 1 mM sample of the SaSufS-Co2+-SaSufU complex exhibits a reduced maximum intensity  and FT intensities, and in this case, results in a substantial and obvious change to the EXAFS (Fig. 7b). The EXAFS oscillations clearly show a beat pattern minimum at k ~ 9 while the two FT peaks are now essentially equal in magnitude. Curve fitting (Table 1) suggests that only 2 Co S ligands are now present at an average Co S distance of 2.24 A. However, the Debye-Waller factor for this interaction is relatively large, with sigma2 = 0.0088 A2, equivalent to sigma = 0.09 A. This is close to the distance resolution of 0.11 A and likely reflects either disorder or different Co S distances within the Co S shell. The Co-O/N shell is best fit by three Co O or Co N ligands. EXAFS cannot normally distinguish backscattering elements within an atomic number, meaning that a Co-O/N interaction could also be a Co N interaction. Bearing that caveat in mind, and with prior knowledge of the metal-binding pocket, we have fit the Co2+-SaSufU-SaSufS complex EXAFS with a Co O interaction at 1.89 A, a Co N interaction at 2.02 A and a Co O interaction at 2.16 A. This result can be rationalized in terms of the loss of one Co S interaction and the gain of a Co N interaction. This is consistent with the replacement of cysteine by histidine proposed to occur in the BsSufU-BsSufS complex. Collectively, these data suggest a Cys2ApsHis ligand environment for Co2+ where the Asp ligand possesses bi-dentate coordination or possibly a Cys2ApsHisH2O ligand environment.

Reaction of 3 mM cysteine with Co(II)-SaSufU-SaSufS for 90 s before freezing in the EXAFS cuvette causes further but less dramatic changes to the EXAFS spectrum (Fig. 7c). These data are best seen in the FT spectrum, which shows an increase in intensity for both peaks. Curve fitting reveals a similar structure to the Co(II)-SaSufU-SaSufS sample, with 3 Co-O/N and 2 Co-S; however, the Co S shell has a lower Debye-Waller factor at with sigma2 = 0.0057 A2, suggesting a more ordered active site with a change in the cysteine ligands. This may well be the catalytic cysteine acquiring a persulfide group. Finally, the Co FT EXAFS data show significant structure at longer distances, R > 2.6 A. These features arise from interactions with non-ligand amino-acid atoms within the pocket, such as amino-acid beta-carbons and the imidazole ring atoms of histidine. While the signal-to-noise of the current data set limits our analysis of this region, future fitting of these FT features will provide additional insight into the structural changes within the Co2+ ion first coordination sphere.
Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)

The electronic properties of the active site Co2+ ion in SaSufU were further examined via EPR spectroscopy (Fig. 8). The EPR spectrum of a 1 mM Co2+-SaSufU sample was obtained at 13 K and 2 mW microwave power (Fig. 8A) and derives from an  doublet of an  spin system with an essentially axial zero-field splitting tensor. These data are typical of 5- or 6-coordinate Co2+ centers that have one or more water ligands as reported for a number of Co2+-substituted metallohydrolases. At lower temperature and higher microwave power (7 K, 100 mW), this signal was diminished in intensity and severely distorted due to saturation and rapid-passage effects, respectively, but a new, fast-relaxing species was observed with a sharp peak at 1095 G (g' = 6.2) (Fig. 8D). This observed temperature and power dependence of signals with distinct resonances and relaxation behaviors is very similar to that observed upon the addition of the inhibitor L-leucinethiol (LeuSH) to a Co2+-substituted aminopeptidase. It is also qualitatively similar to those observed for other thiol inhibitors, whereas the analogous leucenol did not elicit a fast-relaxing signal of the type seen here, since there is not a thiol group present in leucenol. The fast-relaxing signal of Co2+-SaSufU itself is also very similar to that of the Co2+-substituted aminopeptidase bound by LeuSH, in which a water ligand is replaced by an S- ligand from LeuSH. Thus, these data strongly suggest that the presence of the low-temperature signal is an indicator of thiol coordination. In the case of the Co2+-substituted aminopeptidase-LeuSH complex, the signal was interpreted as most likely arising from the  doublet of an  spin system, likely due to a 4- or 5-coordinated thiol-bound Co2+ center. This interpretation was supported by comparison with other systems and from the d-d transitions in the UV-Vis spectrum and EXAFS data. This interpretation also holds for Co2+-SaSufU for the same reasons. The difference between the two species responsible for the two distinct EPR signals (temperature and power dependent) may be due to either differences in the nature of the oxygen environment, e.g. bidentate Asp coordination vs monodentate Asp coordination plus a water ligand, or by differences in the sulfur environment. The heterogeneity in the Co2+ coordination revealed by EPR spectroscopy is supported by the disparate EXAFS-derived cobalt-ligand atom distances within each of the S and O scattering shells and by the non-integral numbers of S scatterers required to obtain the best fit. The residual derivative feature at 1500 G in the spectrum of Fig. 8D is due to the rapid-passage signal from the slow-relaxing species. An additional small signal was observed at 450 G (g' ~ 13) that was reminiscent of an integer spin signal but gave no EPR signal with B0 B, and its origin remains unclear.

Upon the addition of SaSufS, a small change (Fig. 8B) in the slow-relaxing signal was observed, indicating a small geometric and/or ligand environment rearrangement. Based on the EXAFS data, we propose that this could be due to the replacement of the Cys41 ligand in Co2+-SaSufU with His349 of SaSufS, like that proposed for BsSufU but could also be due to small geometric changes in the Co2+ environment due to SaSufS-SaSufU complex formation. At 7 K and 100 mW (Fig. 8E), there was a similarly slight change in the EPR spectrum, with a shift of the maximum from g' = 6.2 to 6.3. These data suggest a small but detectable change in the Co2+ coordination environment. The residual derivative feature in the 7 K spectrum of Co2+-SaSufU at 1500 G, due to the rapid-passage signal from the slow-relaxing species, was extinguished upon the addition of SaSufS, indicating even slower relaxation of that signal. In this case, the presence of two distinct EPR species is not directly confirmed by a need for non-integral numbers of scatterers in the EXAFS fit, though the heterogeneity in distances within the N/O scattering shell is still suggestive.
Conclusion

The absence of X-ray crystallographic information for SaSufU and the lack of solution data supporting a Zn2+-ligand swapping mechanism prompted us to prepare the spectroscopically rich Co2+-substituted SaSufU enzyme. Co2+-SaSufU stimulated SaSufS activity ~2-fold compared to ~10-fold for Zn2+-SaSufU, indicating Co2+-SaSufU can enhance the cysteine desulfurase activity of SaSufS. Electronic absorption data indicate the Co2+ bound to SaSufU resides in either a distorted four- or five-coordinate geometry with a Cys3Asp ligand set. The fifth ligand is likely due to bidentate Asp ligand coordination, as previously observed, but a water molecule cannot be ruled out. Titration of Co2+ into apo-SaSufU provided an upper limit for a  value of ~600 nM, suggesting that Co2+ binds to the active site of SaSufU rather strongly, but still weaker than Zn2+. Zn K-edge absorption spectra (XAS) could be reasonably fit to 1 N/O scatterer at 2.04 A and 3 S scatterers at 2.32 A. These data are consistent with a distorted tetrahedral coordination environment for Zn2+, likely Cys3Asp, which is identical to that of BsSufU. Replacement of the Zn2+ with Co2+ in SaSufU results in a five-coordinate active site, likely due to bidentate Asp coordination or possibly a water molecule, with one of the cysteines moving about 0.2 A further away from the Co2+ ion. Binding of SaSufS modifies this coordination, introducing the partial addition of an N or O ligand in the Zn2+ EXAFS spectrum, most likely a histidine, accompanied by the loss of a cysteine, consistent with the proposed ligand-swapping mechanism. EPR data are consistent with a small but detectable change in the Co2+ coordination environment that could be due to replacement of the Cys41 ligand in Co2+-SaSufU with His349 of SaSufS, like that proposed for BsSufU but could also be due to small geometric changes in the Co2+ environment due only to SaSufS-SaSufU complex formation. The latter is consistent with UV-Vis data, which do not suggest a ligand-swap upon the addition of SaSufS to Co2+-SaSufU as no change in the intensity of the 340 nm band due to a S-   Co(II) LMCT is observed, nor are the d-d bands between 500 and 800 nm significantly perturbed. However, UV-Vis data obtained after incubation with Cys suggest ligand-swapping in the SaSufS-Co2+-SaSufU complex (Fig. 9). This perceived difference in the situational requirements for SaSufS-SaSufU complex ligand-swapping interestingly suggests a dependence on enzyme concentration, as the UV-Vis data were obtained using 150 muM samples vs. 1 mM samples for EXAFS and EPR. At high concentrations, including crystallization experiments, His349 in SaSufS appears to displace Cys41 as a Zn2+ ligand in SaSufU even in the absence of cysteine; however, at lower concentrations of SaSufS-SaSufU, such as those used in the UV-Vis experiments, no ligand swapping is observed. This hints at the possibility of allosteric regulation of the SaSufS-SaSufU sulfide transfer process mediated by cysteine. At low enzyme concentrations, the data presented herein suggest that, in addition to acting as a substrate, Cys may function as a switch for the SaSufS-SaSufU complex, affecting the through-space transformations requisite to SaSufS-SaSufU Zn2+ ligand swapping. Such a switch would ultimately be responsible for driving ligand swapping, even at relatively low physiological enzyme concentrations.

passages.text: Machine learning-based development of Gadolinium binding peptides

Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) are indispensable tools in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), yet their clinical use is limited by non-specific tissue accumulation, low molecular specificity, and safety concerns. Protein and peptide scaffolds provide a promising alternative because they can bind metal ions with high selectivity and enable precise molecular targeting. However, identifying short peptide motifs with optimal gadolinium (Gd3+) coordination and high relaxivity remains a major challenge.

Here, we used a machine-learning-driven peptide evolution platform, the Protein Optimization Engineering Tool (POET), to design and optimize short Gd-binding motifs that enhance longitudinal relaxivity (r1). Two algorithmic strategies were tested; motif-based and regular-expression-based representations, both were trained on an initial set of 74 twelve-amino-acid peptides derived from natural EF-hand scaffolds. Through two rounds of directed evolution and experimental screening, we identified peptides with up to a 24% increase in r1 ratio compared with the best natural EF-hand, and a 55% improvement in absolute r1 after removal of unbound Gd.

Further analysis revealed that peptides exhibiting higher relaxivity generally possessed a more negative net charge and lower isoelectric point than the buffer pH, indicating stronger electrostatic stabilization of Gd3+. Sequence enrichment analysis showed that acidic and small polar residues, particularly aspartic acid, glycine, and threonine, were selectively favored during evolution, while bulky hydrophobic and basic residues were depleted. These compositional trends align with improved solubility and enhanced metal coordination.

Together, these results demonstrate a generalizable framework that integrates computational evolution with biophysical screening to discover new biologically derived Gd-binding motifs. This approach provides a scalable route to engineer responsive, tunable, and biocompatible MRI contrast tags for precision imaging and molecular diagnostics.
INTRODUCTION

Gd is a rare earth element (REE) and one of fifteen lanthanide group elements. Gd's electron configuration makes it highly reactive, and it enhances proton relaxation to create a high magnetic moment making it an ideal element for an MRI contrast agent. Since 1988, gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) have been developed to improve stability and reduce toxicity, but they have remained the predominant choice as high-quality contrast imaging agents. The negative aspect of GBCAs is that they are a broad contrast agent administered into the blood stream in order to disperse throughout the entire body, which has been shown to cause other adverse effects such as accumulation in skin, muscle, bone, and brain. One of the reasons Gd accumulates in the body is that the Gd cation (Gd+3), when unchelated, has biophysical characteristics similar to Ca+2, and several studies have investigated the potential mimicry effects this may have on body systems. Research found that Gd+3 ions increased mitochondrial fluidity, resulting in promotion of apoptosis in mice livers, contributing to further suspicions of unknown toxicities of Gd in the body. Previous research has also shown that the binding of GdCl3 to tubulin of NIH-3T3 cells might inhibit the assembly of tubulin or depolymerize microtubules in cells, while the GBCA gadolinium diamide (gadodiamide) showed much lower levels of toxicity. That being said, studies have shown GBCAs are not as inert to protein binding as many assume, demonstrating that more work must be done to understand the implications that weak but broad protein binding may have in vivo. Therefore, it is extremely desirable to develop GBCAs that are more efficient, reducing the amount of potential harmful metal administered to patients.

passages.text: Biologics are substances and products derived from living organisms that are used to prevent, diagnose, or treat a variety of health conditions. In randomized control trials, biologics have demonstrated an ability to improve quality of life for patients suffering from joint damage, skin lesions, and gastrointestinal inflammation. Not only have biologics demonstrated potential to be effective pharmacological agents in chronic disease, but they also present opportunities for increased precision and tailoring to patient needs. It is highly desirable to track biologics in vivo as part of theranostics therapies, since it is important to know whether the biologic reached its target in the body. GBCAs have been used to track biologics using MRI, with most efforts targeting chemical conjugation of GBCA to the biologic. However, attaching Gd chelates to antibodies, for example, often produces heterogeneous labeling, leading to variable relaxivity, impaired binding, and reduced immunoreactivity. Because each chelate contributes only modestly to the MRI signal, multiple Gd units are required, complicating synthesis, purification, and reproducibility.

By contrast, biologics-based scaffolds provide a more controlled alternative. For example, lanmodulin, a recently discovered bacterial protein with picomolar affinity and 108-fold selectivity for lanthanides over Ca2+, coordinates lanthanides using EF-hand motifs, short helix-loop-helix structures that typically bind Ca2+ in the calmodulin protein. In lanmodulin, four EF hands have been adapted for lanthanide binding, providing a natural, high-affinity scaffold for engineering next-generation GBCAs. Engineered variants such as the single-point mutated LanND-Gd, achieve longitudinal relaxivity of 13.15 mM-1 s-1 at 3 T, significantly higher than that of the clinically used agent Magnevist (4.62 mM-1 s-1 at 3 T).

Another prominent biologics-based platform is the Protein Contrast Agent (ProCA) series, ProCA32, a third-generation protein GBCA based on calmodulin with engineered EF-hand motifs, which achieves r1 values of ~33 mM-1 s-1 at 1.4 T and 37  C, nearly tenfold higher than Magnevist (3.3 mM-1 s-1 under identical conditions). ProCA32 can also be fused with targeting moieties (e.g., HER2, EGFR, VEGFR) without compromising metal coordination, enabling high-sensitivity molecular imaging of cancers, fibrosis, and metastases in vivo.

Together, LanND-Gd and ProCA32 show how protein scaffolds can deliver an order-of-magnitude boost in relaxivity while preserving targeting and stability. By tightly coordinating Gd3+ within EF-hand motifs, these biologics minimize metal release and enable fusion with recognition domains, making them potentially powerful platforms for high-sensitivity, clinically relevant molecular imaging.

Despite these advances, current protein-based GBCA remain limited by the need to optimize metal-binding motifs for maximal relaxivity in a systematic, predictive manner. Most efforts rely on single-point mutations or rational design, which can be laborious and may miss nonintuitive sequence combinations that could further enhance performance. There is a clear need for computational tools that can efficiently explore the vast sequence space of short motifs, learn sequence-function relationships, and propose variants with improved relaxivity and binding properties.

Here we address this gap by applying POET (Protein Optimization Engineering Tool), a genetic programming-based algorithm, to systematically explore and optimize lanthanide binding peptides. POET has already been successfully applied to optimize short amino acid motifs for chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI applications, demonstrating its ability to efficiently explore sequence space and uncover nonintuitive variants with enhanced performance. POET has two versions which use different methods to recognize amino acid sequences. The original POET (called here POETmotif) in which individuals are composed of amino acid subsequences paired with corresponding weights, and an extension of POET (called here POETregex) where individuals are represented by a list of regular expressions (regex) and corresponding weights.

Our objectives in the present work were to (i) discover short motifs with improved r1 relative to natural EF-hand using a high-throughput assay, and (ii) compare POETmotif and POETregex to assess efficiency and diversity of outputs. More broadly, we aimed to establish a pipeline for motif discovery that could inform the design of next-generation protein-based MRI contrast agents.
METHODS
Peptide Synthesis and Preparation

The peptides were purchased from Genscript USA Inc. (Piscataway, NJ). HEPES ((4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid)) and GdCl3 were purchased from Thermo Scientific Chemicals, Waltham, MA USA. HEPES was chosen because other buffers containing phosphates tend to form Gd-phosphate sediments.
MRI measurements

The ability of a contrast agent (CA) to produce MRI contrast is quantified by relaxivity, which is the CA's ability to change the relaxation rate of a solution as a function of its concentration. To measure relaxivity one must measure the longitudinal relaxation time (T1) of several dilutions of the CA, and extract the slope from linear regression of the following equation

Where  and  are the longitudinal relaxation time of the solution with and without the CA respectively.  is the longitudinal relaxivity and [CA] is the GdCl3 concentration of the CA measured by inductively coupled plasma (ICP) (Varian 710-ES). ICP samples were prepared by nitric acid digestion.

Peptides were dissolved in HEPES 50mM and GdCl3 0.2mM pH 5.3 and incubated r1 = r1 (peptide)/r1 (GdCl3)) measurements the samples were diluted to measure their T1 values, along with GdCl3 that did not have any peptide. To perform more high-throughput measurements, Gd concentrations were not measured for these peptides. Instead, the peptides' r1 were divided by the peptide-free Gd r1. For absolute relaxivity, MRI was conducted 42 hours after incubation with GdCl3 and two dialysis cycles.

To create a series of dilutions, an epMotion 5073 liquid handler was used to ensure pipetting accuracy. The sample, along with 6 or 7 sample dilutions and a blank solution, were pipetted into a 396 plate cut to fit inside the MRI magnet bore, sample volume inside the wells was ~100 microliters. 7 columns along the phase axis and 5 rows along the read axis could be measured with a relatively homogeneous field. Two custom fitted plates were stacked on top of each other, enabling measurements of two slices simultaneously.

MRI measurements were performed on a horizontal 30 cm bore 7 T Bruker preclinical MRI with ParaVision 360 v3.2 on a Linux computer running CentOS7, using a B-GA12SHP high performance gradient insert with built-in shims. A variable repetition time T1 map was acquired using a RARE sequence with 9 TRs (33 122 297 497 727 1577 2777 4809 12496) ms/TE 6.88 ms, RARE factor = 1, FOV ~ 40x25 mm, with the matrix adjusted to ensure a spatial resolution of 0.25x0.25 mm, slice thickness = 1.2 mm, 1 or 2 slices, echo spacing was 6.88 ms. This is correlated to measurement times of 40 to 60 minutes. Finally, the T1 for each well was measured using the image sequence analysis module in Paravision, then r1 ratio or absolute r1 relaxivity were calculated.
Peptide evolution using machine learning

Two versions of the POET algorithm were compared for their ability to create peptides that can shorten the T1 relaxation of water and have higher r1 ratio. POETmotif and POETregex., the former using motifs represented as substrings, and the latter using regular expressions (regex), a formal way of defining a set of character sequences. A motif/regex was classified as beneficial when it had r1 ratio > 1, which corresponds to the r1 ratio of GdCl3 without a peptide. POET uses a form of supervised training called Genetic Programming. Each POET trial generates a set of rules that determine r1 ratio by checking the composition of a proposed peptide sequence. If a given motif (or regex) is found, the corresponding weight is added to a sum value, in this case r1 ratio. The rulesets interact through recombination and mutation over timesteps (called generations), and once all generations are completed, the most accurate model is returned for peptide generation. Both POET variants were trained with 74 12-amino acid long peptides incubated with GdCl3. The r1 of the peptides was normalized to the r1 of the buffer with the same amount of GdCl3.
Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements

Solution NMR experiments were carried out on a 600 MHz Bruker Avance NEO NMR spectrometer equipped with a 5 mm Prodigy TCI cryoprobe. 1H NMR experiments were run at 25 C using the vendor supplied water suppression pulse sequence (noesygppr1d) to measure 1H spectra of 1mM peptide of EF3 and CaBM. Both peptides were suspended in HEPES 50mM with 10% D2O for locking, shimming, and chemical shift referencing with or without 5muM GdCl3.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Peptide evolution

Both POET algorithms were applied to evolve Gd-binding peptides with enhanced MRI relaxivity. Figure 1 and S1 show plots of the r1 ratio of the peptides predicted by POETmotif and POETregex over two POET cycles dubbed Epoch 1 and 2. In Figure 1 the red dashed line represents the r1 ratio of EF hand 3 motif (EF3) (r1=1.86), a 12-amino-acid from Lanmodulin that showed the highest r1 ratio from the training data. For the POETmotif in Epoch 1, only three peptides showed better contrast than the EF3 peptide; however, in Epoch 2, 9 of 10 peptides surpassed the r1 ratio of the EF3 hand peptide. For POETregex 7 out of 10 peptides surpassed the r1 ratio of EF3 in both Epochs 1 and 2. The best motif found had an r1 ratio of 2.3, a 24.3% improvement over the EF3. Peptides displaying an r1 relaxivity ratio lower than that of EF3 suggest that POET did not have sufficient data to fully explore the sequence space. Nevertheless, the algorithm successfully identified novel peptides with enhanced relaxivity, demonstrating its capacity to discover functionally improved motifs beyond those found in nature. Next, the correlation between POET's predictions and MRI measurements was examined. No correlations were observed, indicating that more epochs could improve the correlation.
Validation of the Gd-relaxivity

The r1 ratio is a convenient high-throughput metric reflecting the ability of Gd-binding peptides to enhance longitudinal relaxivity; however, it represents combined contributions from peptide-bound and free Gd3+ ions. To verify this and to characterize the metal species present prior to dialysis, we performed electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy (Supporting Information, Figure S1). The dialyzed EF3 sample exhibited a broad, downfield-shifted, low-intensity ESR signal characteristic of peptide-bound Gd3+. In contrast, the undialyzed EF3 + Gd3+ mixture, after subtraction of the free-Gd spectrum, displayed a strong residual central peak and a downfield shoulder. The central peak reflects an incomplete cancellation of the intense free-Gd transition, while the shoulder represents a heterogeneous population of Gd3+ interacting with the peptide. The distinct downfield positions of the two traces indicate that the bound Gd3+ species present before and after dialysis occupy slightly different electronic environments due to differences in exchange, hydration, and coordination equilibrium. These ESR results show that undialyzed samples contain a large fraction of free Gd3+ with a different electronic environment than the peptide-bound species observed after dialysis. Therefore, we measured absolute r1 after dialysis to confirm that it correlates with the r1 ratio used in the initial screen.

With this rationale, the absolute relaxivities (r1) of Gd-binding peptides were measured after two cycles of dialysis over 48 hours against HEPES buffer to remove excess Gd3+, which typically reduced the total Gd concentration from 0.2 mM to ~20 muM. Peptides showing a range of r1 ratios (Table 1) were selected, including EF-hand motifs, a calcium-binding motif (CaBM) peptide, a lanthanide-binding peptide, and peptides predicted by POET. A strong correlation was found between the r1 ratio and absolute r1 (Figure 2; R2 = 0.6137, p = 0.0073). These findings indicate that r1 ratio is a reliable predictor of absolute relaxivity and can be used as an efficient screening metric to minimize time and material use. Moreover, when comparing absolute r1 values, a 42.6% improvement was observed for the best peptide identified in the initial screening (IDCRGTEDDDPN) relative to EF3, versus the 24.3% improvement indicated by its r1 ratio. The peptide showing the highest absolute r1 (TQDSDDGMEDED) displayed a 55.2% enhancement over EF3. Taken together, these results demonstrate that POET can successfully identify novel peptides that coordinate Gd3+ and achieve relaxivities exceeding those of natural sequences.
Analysis of peptide's isoelectric point and net charge

After two Epochs, an extensive analysis was performed to evaluate POET's predicted peptides. First, the net charge and the isoelectric point (IP) at pH 5.3 were calculated for each peptide and plotted against their r1 ratio. The results in Figure 3 show that most peptides with an r1 ratio better than free-Gd had a negative net charge, and usually the r1 ratio improved with more negative net charge, since Gd has a 3+ positive charge this makes sense. For the IP, peptides with values under 5.3 had higher r1 ratios, since the buffer's pH was 5.3, only peptides with lower IP had negative charges that could stabilize the Gd3+ ions. The results suggest that for further evolution, the peptides' net charge should be negative, and their IP should be lower than the buffer's pH, both conditions easily screened using POET. It is possible that some motifs and regular expressions were neglected by POET because the net charge of the molecule was too high, so it could be beneficial for future Epochs to use only the negatively charged peptides. It could also be useful to choose the buffer pH to be as high as possible, leading peptides that have higher IP to have higher r1 values, making the dataset more helpful for learning in POET.
Paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE)

PRE measurements were performed to validate that Gd binds to the peptides, and to investigate which amino acids are more involved in the binding. A comparison was made between similar EF-hands, EF3, known to bind lanthanides, and CaBM, known to bind Calcium.

Since Gd3+ is a paramagnetic ion that significantly shortens both the T1 and T2 of any NMR active nuclei within approximately 25 angstroms of the binding site, NMR was used to measure 1H spectra of 1mM peptide of EF3 and CaBM with or without 5muM GdCl3. As shown in Figure 4, EF3 displays a more significant increase in the linewidths of all proton peaks with a concomitant reduction in intensity due to paramagnetic relaxation than those of CaBM. PRE will be more pronounced for those protons proximal to the binding site than for those distal, which is why EF3 displays more significant broadening of the NH peaks of Asp-D, Gly-G, Leu-L, and Thr-T (7.9-8.4 ppm) than other proton resonances in the peptide. CaBM also displays broadening for Asp-D, Gly-G, Ser-S, and Glu-E, but to a lesser extent, and there is comparatively little relaxation enhancement for the aliphatic protons of leucine (0.95 and 1.6 ppm) thereby indicating that these protons are more distal to the Gd binding sites. The number of NH resonances broadened into the baseline is higher for EF3 than CaBM which can be attributed to a higher percentage of amino acids binding to Gd for EF3 than CaBM.
Amino acid distribution

The performances of POETmotif and POETregex were evaluated and compared by the amino acid composition of each algorithm and Epoch. Figure 5A shows the distribution of the different amino-acids classes within the resulting peptide sequences, Acidic (D, E), Basic (K, H, R), Aliphatic (A, G, I, L, P, V), Aromatic (F, W, Y), Hydroxylic (S, T), Sulfur-containing (C, M) and Amidic (N, Q). Figure 5B illustrates the individual amino acid distribution. Importantly, the initial training dataset exhibited a nearly uniform distribution of amino acid residues, providing an unbiased starting point for the evolution performed by POET.

Across all groups, there was a consistent and pronounced enrichment of acidic residues (particularly aspartic acid, D) and a marked depletion of basic amino acids (notably lysine, K, and arginine, R). This suggests a strong selection for negatively charged residues capable of coordinating with the positively charged Gd3+ ions, and simultaneous avoidance of positively charged residues to minimize electrostatic repulsion. Aspartic acid emerged as the dominant residue in both, motif and regex patterns during both evolutionary epochs, comprising over 24% of amino acids in all of POET's outputs. This selection mirrors the composition of many natural EF-hand motifs, which often contain multiple aspartic acids involved in metal ion coordination. While there was a general reduction in non-polar aliphatic residues, one exception was glycine (G), which increased significantly in Epoch 2 motifs. Glycine's small side chain likely contributes to increased peptide flexibility and solubility, properties that may be advantageous in a hydrophilic or dynamic binding context. The hydroxylic class (serine and threonine) showed moderate enrichment, particularly threonine (T), which rose sharply in Epoch 1 Motif. These residues support hydrogen bonding and surface polarity, reinforcing the hydrophilic nature of the evolving peptides.

The aromatic and basic classes, especially phenylalanine (F), tryptophan (W), and lysine (K), were consistently depleted across all outputs, indicating a preference against bulky, hydrophobic, or positively charged side chains. Sulfur-containing and amidic residues (C, M, N, Q) exhibited more subtle variations, with no strong trend in either direction.

Consistent with these compositional trends, PRE measurements confirmed that several of the amino acids enriched by POET are indeed directly involved in Gd3+ coordination. In particular, residues such as aspartic acid (D), glycine (G), and threonine (T), which showed strong enrichment in the evolved sequences, were among those that exhibited significant signal broadening in EF-hand peptides upon Gd binding.

Notably, the inclusion of all 20 amino acids in the training set allowed POET to explore a broad sequence space during motif and regex discovery, enabling the algorithm to converge on a highly specific and chemically coherent set of residue preferences aligned with metal-binding functionality.
CONCLUSION

We applied POET to expand and optimize short lanthanide-binding peptide motifs and demonstrate a practical, data-driven route to improve Gd-mediated T1 contrast. Starting from an experimental library of 74 sequences and using iterative POET cycles, we identified novel peptides with substantially enhanced relaxivity, the best POET-predicted motif yielded an r1-ratio of 2.30 (~24% higher than the best initial EF-hand, EF3), and top peptides measured after dialysis showed up to ~55% higher absolute r1 than EF3. The screening metric (r1 ratio) correlated with absolute relaxivity (R2 ~ 0.61, p ~ 0.007), validating the high-throughput screening approach, and PRE spectra support that Gd3+ is in proximity to peptide residues. Sequence analysis revealed strong enrichment of acidic residues (notably Asp), consistent with electrostatic and coordinating roles in Gd binding.

These findings show that coupling POET with a high-throughput r1 screening can efficiently explore short-motif sequence space and produce superior candidates; and that running complementary POET recognition modes (motif and regex) yields both rapid consensus improvements and broader, nonintuitive solutions. Some discovered peptides could be explored as standalone contrast agents; future work will evaluate motif transferability into full proteins (e.g., Lanmodulin) and biologics (e.g., antibodies). Overall, POET combined with a high-throughput pipeline provides the foundation for designing peptide tags and for guiding the development of next-generation biologics-based Gd MRI contrast agents with improved sensitivity and translational potential.

passages.text: Polarity effects, resistance, and probiotic enhancement of intoxication of Salmonella enterica fraB mutants in murine models

FraB is a deglycase in a metabolic pathway that allows Salmonella to utilize fructose-asparagine (F-Asn). Some fraB mutants are sensitive to F-Asn due to the accumulation of 6-phosphofructose-aspartate (6-P-F-Asp), a toxic intermediate in this pathway. We determined that different alleles of fraB cause different amounts of 6-P-F-Asp-mediated toxicity due to effects on the expression of the downstream gene, fraD, a kinase. Mutations in fraD or fraA (a transporter) cause resistance to F-Asn intoxication, and these mutations occur during infection. To better mimic the effect of a hypothetical FraB inhibitor in mouse models, we characterized a non-polar mutant encoding a catalytically inactive FraB (FraB E214A). We also compared a typical mouse chow and a high-fat chow and found that the latter decreases the variation in colonization typically observed during infection of CBA/J mice with Salmonella. Because the high-fat chow lacks F-Asn, the fraB E214A mutant was not attenuated in mice fed this diet unless F-Asn was supplemented. F-Asn supplementation resulted in a 100-fold reduction of colony forming units (CFU) recovered from feces compared to wild-type. Co-infection of Salmonella with a Salmonella "probiotic" strain that is neither virulent nor capable of consuming F-Asn (a SPI1 SPI2 fraR-BDAE ansB mutant) led to a dramatic 10,000-fold reduction in CFU and a 1000-fold reduction in lipocalin-2, a proxy marker of inflammation. This probiotic strain presumably competes for nutrients other than F-Asn, driving the fraB mutant to consume a higher proportion of F-Asn and greater 6-P-F-Asp intoxication. Thus, a putative inhibitor of FraB, when administered with F-Asn and a probiotic, may provide a new therapeutic strategy for treating Salmonella gastroenteritis.
